How Much Of Comcast Stock Rides On One Shrinking Number?
sum: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Comcast (CMCSA) is keeping less of each sales dollar as operating profit than it used to. Its operating margin fell to 14.7% over the twelve months to September 2026, from 18.0% a year earlier. That matters because Comcast’s sales were flat at $123 billion, so any change in its operating profit now comes from its margin. So what is pulling Comcast’s margin down?

Management says Comcast is paying to defend its broadband business. On the October 22, 2026 call, management said fixed wireless rivals keep taking share and fiber construction remains elevated, and that the results reflect what Comcast is spending to fight back, including new pricing and packaging. Management called that spending a near-term financial pressure, and said the changes made over the past year still weigh on results.

The theme parks have added to the pressure. Theme park EBITDA, management’s measure of profit before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, fell 17% in the quarter, mainly because of softness in Orlando that began in June and travel restrictions weighing on its business in Japan, management said.

On the twelve-month measure, Comcast’s margin has fallen three years in a row, down from 19.3% in the twelve months to September 2023. It was 18.5% a year after that. The margin peaked at 21.5% in fiscal Q3 2017. Across the 40 quarter-ends since the end of 2016, it was lower than today only once.
At Comcast’s current sales, each percentage point of margin is worth about $1.2 billion of operating income a year.

Comcast stock trades at 7.8 times its last twelve months of earnings, against 21.9 for the S&P 500. Over the twelve months to November 12, 2026, the shares returned 1.4%, against 12.2% for the S&P 500.

What Could Go Wrong At Comcast From Here?
sum: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Comcast (CMCSA) stock trades at 7.8 times its earnings over the last twelve months, compared with 22.3 for the S&P 500. A price that low appears to assume trouble ahead. Management pointed to a potential source of that trouble during its October 22, 2026 call, saying the company has operated in an intensely competitive environment for some time. So who is coming after Comcast’s customers, and how hard are they pushing?
Fiber And Fixed Wireless Rivals Are Taking Comcast’s Customers

Management said so itself on the fiscal Q3 2026 call. It said fixed wireless remains aggressive and continues to take share, while fiber construction remains elevated, with pockets of irrational pricing.

The company also explained why it calls some of that pricing irrational. Building fiber costs $1,500 or more per home, management said, yet rivals offered $30 to $40 pricing in specific markets in the third quarter.

Broadband sits in Comcast’s largest segment, Residential Connectivity & Platforms, which brought in $70.7 billion of revenue in fiscal 2025, more than any other segment. That revenue, 57.2% of Comcast’s total, fell 1.2% in fiscal 2025, more than double the 0.5% dip in fiscal 2024, so the segment’s slow decline is speeding up. That figure covers the whole segment, so it is wider than broadband revenue alone.

The share price already sits low against Comcast’s own history. The stock trades at 0.715 times its sales over the last twelve months, against a high of 2.4 times at the end of June 2021. At the end of September 2026, the multiple was 0.629 times, its lowest at any quarter end from late 2016 on. Even after a strong month, on November 10 the stock closed 20.6% below its highest close of the past year. The price appears to assume little growth from here.

Comcast Yields 5.6% and Trades at Just 8 Times Earnings. Is It a Trap?
sum: - Comcast (CMCSA) pays out just 28% of free cash flow in dividends, leaving a wide cushion despite a 5.58% yield and shares down 43% over five years.
- Charter (CHTR) lost 233,000 internet customers and pays no dividend, while Disney (DIS) trades near 16 times earnings, making Comcast's discount look wider.
- Comcast lost 144,000 broadband customers in Q3 as fixed wireless takes share, yet wireless service revenue rose 15% and Peacock turned profitable.

Comcast (NASDAQ:CMCSA) pays a 5.58% dividend yield and trades at roughly 8 times earnings. That is a high yield and a low multiple. The market has priced it this way for a while: shares are down 9.02% year-to-date and 43.03% over five years.

A value trap is a stock that looks cheap because the business behind it is shrinking, so the price keeps slipping, earnings decline, and the dividend that drew you in eventually gets cut. Retirees feel this most. They lose both income and principal (we listed seven warning signs that a big yield is about to be cut in a free report).

In Q3, Comcast generated $4.211B in free cash flow and paid $1.2B in dividends. That works out to about 28% of free cash flow. The $1.32 annual dividend uses about 35% of the past four quarters of adjusted EPS. The quarterly payout has risen from $0.1575 in 2017 to $0.33. It has stayed flat through 2026, though, and the next payment is also $0.33.

Comcast stock weighs strong cash flow against broadband losses
sum: Comcast is generating substantial cash, but its broadband business is losing customers and its balance sheet remains a central issue for investors. A Trefis analysis published by Yahoo Finance on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, said Comcast produced 17.1 billion US dollars in free cash flow over the twelve months through September.

Free cash flow stayed positive in each of the 13 twelve-month periods ending between September 2023 and September 2026, according to the analysis. The figure reached 18.1 billion US dollars in the twelve months through September 2025, up from 11.0 billion US dollars a year earlier, before easing in the latest period.

There were offsets. Wireless lines increased 18 percent year over year, and management expects the cost overhaul to generate billions of dollars over time. Theme-park revenue, however, fell 4 percent in the third quarter, with Orlando and Japan identified as weak spots.

Leverage remains important because debt holders have a prior claim on cash flow. Comcast's total debt stood at 87.4 billion US dollars at the end of September, down from 99.1 billion US dollars a year earlier. The analysis said operating income covered interest expense 4.3 times over the twelve months through September.

Management expects fourth-quarter free cash flow to face a reversal of favorable timing effects seen in the third quarter, when the company generated 4.2 billion US dollars. Comcast also expects a charge of more than 1 billion US dollars, largely linked to its cost transformation program.

The planned separation of the NBCUniversal and Sky businesses is expected to be completed by mid-2027. Management wants both the remaining connectivity company and the separated media company to retain investment-grade credit ratings. That makes debt reduction and recurring cash generation important milestones as the transaction approaches.

Comcast vs. Walt Disney: Which Entertainment Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?
sum: Media and connectivity giants are navigating a landscape defined by streaming competition and shifting consumer habits. Can Comcast (NASDAQ:CMCSA) or Walt Disney (NYSE:DIS) offer the better path for your portfolio in this environment?

Comcast operates as a diversified leader in broadband, wireless, and entertainment, while Disney focuses on its world-class content library and global destination resorts. Both companies are currently repositioning their businesses to capture long-term value as traditional cable television continues to evolve.

Comcast remains one of the largest entities among media stocks, balancing its traditional cable roots with high-tech connectivity. The company serves roughly 50 million customers across the globe, providing high-speed internet through its Xfinity brand and expanding its mobile presence through partnerships with Verizon and T-Mobile. In its latest annual report, filed for its 2025 fiscal year (FY), Comcast highlighted its strategy to integrate entertainment and connectivity through its Universal theme parks and Peacock streaming service.

In FY 2025, revenue reached $123.7 billion, which was essentially flat compared to the previous year. Despite the lack of top-line growth, the company generated net income of $20 billion. This resulted in a net margin of 16.2%, reflecting the core profitability of its broadband and media operations.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 1.1x, which represents total debt divided by shareholder equity. The current ratio, which measures liquidity by dividing current assets by current liabilities, was 0.9x. Furthermore, the company generated $19.2 billion in free cash flow, defined as cash from operations minus capital expenditures.

In FY 2025, ended Sept. 30 of last year, revenue reached $94.4 billion, indicating a growth rate of 3.4% over the prior year. The company reported net income of $12.4 billion for the same period. This performance resulted in a net margin of 13.1%, as the business continues to scale its direct-to-consumer streaming platforms toward consistent profitability.

Is There A Risk Hiding In Comcast Stock’s Latest Results?
sum: For a Comcast (CMCSA) holder, the average revenue per broadband customer is a troubling metric. That figure fell 3.8% in the second quarter of 2026. During the same period, Comcast lost 167,000 broadband customers. This leaves the company with a shrinking internet base where each remaining user generates less revenue on average. So why is Comcast collecting less from each broadband customer?

Management acknowledged that the investment required for this strategic shift is currently weighing on results. Comcast’s adjusted EBITDA, a measure of operating profit, fell 5% in the second quarter. Management cited two reasons for the decline: the broadband transition and the first year of costs for its NBA rights. Over the past twelve months, Comcast’s operating margin was 14.7%. That metric is down from 18.1% a year earlier, marking its lowest level in five years.

During the second-quarter call, management projected modest improvements starting in the third quarter of 2026 as Comcast begins charging for the previously free lines. Management expects a large majority of those users to switch to paid plans once the promotional offers roll off in the second half of 2026. Customer attrition is also slowing. Broadband losses in the second quarter were 34,000 smaller than a year earlier.

Yet the operating environment remains intensely competitive. Management described the broadband market as highly competitive, noting the expansion of fiber networks, aggressive fixed wireless campaigns, and the emergence of satellite as a viable alternative. EBITDA at Comcast’s connectivity business also fell 5.8% in the quarter. Management tied this drop to spending on sales and customer experience.

Comcast stock trades at 6.6 times earnings, compared with 22.5 for the S&P 500. At this valuation, the price likely assumes the current broadband pressures will persist. The stock lost 21% over the past twelve months, while the S&P 500 gained 21%. Historical market shocks provide a mixed picture of how far Comcast might fall. During the 2022 inflation shock and Fed tightening, the stock dropped 42%, compared with 24% for the S&P 500. In the 2025 tariff shock, however, Comcast fell 9.2%, against 19.0% for the broader index.

sum: Comcast (CMCSA) shares climbed more than 3% Monday after NBCUniversal and Alphabet Inc.'s (GOOGL) YouTube unveiled a landmark streaming partnership that will embed Peacock directly into the YouTube Premium subscription tier starting in early 2027. The deal, described as Peacock's largest wholesale distribution agreement to date, will give the NBCUniversal platform access to YouTube Premium's global base of more than 125 million subscribers.

The multi-year agreement, which also extends NBCUniversal's distribution pact with YouTube TV, marks a significant escalation in the bundling wars reshaping the entertainment landscape. Alphabet shares rose 2.5% in afternoon trading as Wall Street digested the strategic implications of merging a traditional media giant's content library with the tech industry's dominant video platform.

Under the terms of the deal, Peacock's full content catalog — including original series such as "Love Island U.S.A.," the Real Housewives franchise, Universal films like the Minions series, and live sports from the NFL and NBA — will be available to U.S. YouTube Premium subscribers directly within the YouTube app. YouTube Premium's standard individual plan costs $15.99 per month following an April 2026 price increase, with entry-level plans starting at $8.99 for the ad-free Premium Lite tier. That makes the bundle cheaper than subscribing to both services separately, as Peacock Premium, the ad-supported tier, costs $10.99 monthly.
Prices for both services reflect increases taken earlier this year: YouTube raised U.S. Premium pricing in April for the first time since 2023, lifting the individual plan from $13.99.

Unlike conventional distribution deals where streaming services are merely bundled together, this agreement will see Peacock's content ingested into YouTube's platform, allowing viewers to access shows and live events without leaving the YouTube ecosystem. The integration represents a novel approach as media companies increasingly experiment with packaging strategies to combat slowing subscriber growth and rising customer acquisition costs.

sum: UPDATED with closing prices. Charter Communications shares plummeted 25.5% Friday, their biggest single-day sell-off, after the company delivered first-quarter results that disappointed Wall Street.
Earnings per share of $9.17 on a diluted basis fell well short of analysts’ consensus estimate of $10.63. Total revenue dipped 1% to $13.6 billion, hitting the Street’s target.
Charter lost 120,000 broadband customers during the quarter, more than twice the decline of 59,000 in the year-earlier period. The downturn was bigger than the 100,000 losses projected by analysts.

Video, for a change, was a less-discouraging area for Charter, which shed 51,000 residential video customers and 60,000 overall. The losses were narrower than the estimated decline of 85,872. Charter’s earnings release credited “simplified pricing and packaging and benefits from the inclusion of programmers’ streaming applications in Spectrum’s expanded basic video packages.”

The number of mobile lines, for both residential and small business customers, increased 17% over the prior-year quarter to reach 12.1 million. The mobile business has been growing significantly for Charter, Comcast and other cable operators. While the segment has been a welcome bonus for the companies, they don’t own wireless spectrum and must rely on wholesale agreements with Verizon and other partners, which limits the upside.

sum: Newly minted Versant Media saw 2025 profit and revenue dip in a first set of financials — reported as if it had separated from Comcast for the full year — as CEO Mark Lazarus announced plans for an MS NOW extension, a CNBC subscription service, a free Fandango AVOD service and delved into the outlook for sports and advertising.

The cable programmer formally split from the Philadelphia media giant in early January but began operating independently last year, laying out out an original content strategy at an investor meeting in December. That includes an MS NOW (formerly MSNBC) subscription membership prodcut and several transactions strengthening Fandango and FAST technology. While anchored in pay TV, that business continues to slow and Versant is focused on diversifying versus acquiring more cable.
The goal ultimately is to move to a 50-50 revenue split with pay TV balanced by higher-growth digital, platform, subscription, AVOD and transactional businesses, a heavy lift.
The numbers: 2025 net income fell 32% last year to $930 million, on a 5.4% dip in revenue to about $7 billion.

The revenue breakdown saw linear distribution dipping 5.4% to about $4.1 billion; advertising off 9% at $1.6 billion; platforms up 3.9% at $826 million (led by Golf Now and Fandango); and content licensing off 8.5% to $193 million. CNBC and USA are the other core brands at Versant, which houses most of the cable networks formerly under NBCUniversal.

With linear TV so challenged, sports and news are key and Lazarus stressed the expansion of USA Sports’ portfolio through new Pac-12 and women’s sports agreements. He said on a call with analysts that the cost looming as the NFL comes to market will lead to bigger media rivals rebalancing their sports portfolios, “which will create opportunities for us.”
NBCUniversal will continue to represent Versant on the ad side for at least the next two years, “and they they and we will decide on the right future strategy for our ad sales,” Lazarus said.
